parts: An entrepreneur is a person who identifies a business opportunity, turns the idea into action, collects resources, sets up and manages a new enterprise and bears its risk. Entrepreneurship is the process of initiating, creating and managing such an enterprise — a creative, risk-bearing activity. Entrepreneurs are moderate (calculated) risk-takers, not gamblers; they are made by training and experience, not only born; they do things differently from others and constantly strive for excellence; and they generate employment for others.

(1) Provides employment — to the entrepreneur and to others, so it reduces unemployment. (2) Contributes to research and development — most innovations come from entrepreneurs. (3) Creates wealth for individuals and the nation, adding goods and services to the economy. (4) Promotes balanced regional development by setting up units in small towns and villages. (5) Raises the standard of living and increases exports. Small enterprises contribute to national development through employment, use of local resources and skills, a large share of production and exports, equitable distribution of income and support to large industries as suppliers.

(1) Initiative — a man of action who seizes opportunities. (2) Willingness to assume risk. (3) Ability to learn from experience — not repeating mistakes. (4) Motivation — the urge to complete what is started, which keeps a small business going through difficulties and inspires employees. (5) Self-confidence. (6) Decision-making ability — right decisions at the right time, so opportunities are not missed and losses are avoided. Also hard work, creativity, alertness and foresight, leadership, and taking responsibility for one's actions. Success depends on both hard work and a good idea. Lack of confidence is not a quality.

(1) Identifying entrepreneurial opportunities — the first function; sensing human needs (food, fashion, education) faster than others. (2) Turning ideas into action — collecting information and setting goals. (3) Feasibility study — assessing market demand, inputs, costs and problems, prepared as a business plan or project report. (4) Resourcing — arranging money, machines, materials and men. (5) Setting up the enterprise — legal formalities, location, premises, machinery. (6) Managing the enterprise — production, men, finance and marketing. (7) Growth and development — setting higher goals. Innovation and risk bearing run through all of these.

Anyone can start a small business — rich or not, educated or not, rural or urban. Factors to consider: (1) arrangement of finance — fixed capital for land, building, machinery and furniture, and working capital for raw materials, wages, rent and bills; sources: own savings, friends and relatives, banks and financial institutions, government schemes (MUDRA, SIDBI); (2) selection of the line of business according to market demand, profitability and risk; (3) choice of the form of organisation — usually sole proprietorship or partnership; (4) location — near raw materials, the market, labour, transport and banking; a retail shop near residential areas; (5) availability of skilled and semi-skilled labour; (6) technology and machinery, sources of raw material, marketing (sales promotion) and legal formalities. A small business needs only a small amount of working capital.
